endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Avoid extrapolating GAI system performance or capabilities from narrow, nonsystematic, and anecdotal assessments.

endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Where device outputs are evaluated against scoring rubrics, such rubrics would be grounded in established clinical guidelines or validated through qualified expert input and fit-for-use within the assessment context

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: The discrete procedural activity used to gather evaluation evidence. Includes penetration testing, adversarial robustness testing, A/B testing, silent testing, and prospective deployment testing.

endorsements.title: Machine learning for healthcare that matters: Reorienting from technical novelty to equitable impact
endorsements.quote: Work to generate standardized adversarial assessments [ 122 ] to probe the vulnerabilities of a given clinical model.

endorsements.title: The PIEE Cycle: A Structured Framework for Red Teaming Large Language Models in Clinical Decision-Making
endorsements.quote: Once training is established, the proposed framework can be formally integrated into institutional AI governance policies, ensuring that all LLM-based clinical tools are subjected to structured safety evaluations prior to deployment.

endorsements.title: When Compliance Is Not Safety: The Regulatory Blind Spot in AI Companion Chatbots
endorsements.quote: At a minimum, this should include independent evaluation of companion chatbots using standardized youth crisis scenarios, red-team testing by external auditors with clinical and developmental expertise, longitudinal assessment of safety performance across major system updates, and verification that crisis responses and referrals are appropriate to the user's jurisdiction and language.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence in traumatic stress treatment: The TRUST framework for ethical development, clinical applications, and research advancement
endorsements.quote: Predeployment strategies should include training models on diverse, representative datasets; conducting audits across demographic subgroups and trauma types to prioritize equity; implementing “jailbreaking exercises” to identify potential failures and weaknesses; and establishing independent validation processes ( Ferryman et al., 2023 ; Labkoff et al., 2024 ; Welch et al., 2026 ).

endorsements.title: A practical guide to the implementation of AI in orthopaedic research-Part 4: Prerequisites for a successful orthopedics AI-driven project in terms of interdisciplinary collaboration, data management, ethical approval and technology
endorsements.quote: Safety stress‐testing with adversarial inputs (e.g., images with severe metal artefact, pathological anatomy outside the training distribution) must be documented prior to Stage 3 application.

endorsements.title: Responsible and innovative AI for mental health care: five priority themes
endorsements.quote: Independent adversarial testing should explicitly probe psychiatric edge cases, including implicit suicidality, psychosis content, medication misuse, coercion risk, and adolescent vulnerability.

evidence.title: Toward Trustworthy Chatbots: A Protocol for Red Teaming for Health Related Conversations
evidence.outcome: Whether structured red teaming with adversarial probes surfaced vulnerabilities missed by single-turn testing
evidence.effect: Multi-turn stress tests revealed critical vulnerabilities single-turn testing missed; all high-severity errors (4/4) occurred in multi-turn tests.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, multi-turn stress tests revealed critical vulnerabilities that single-turn testing missed, directly informing our choice of targeted mitigations.

evidence.title: Safe Deployment of a Generative AI Assistant for Traditional-Medicine Education: Defense-in-Depth Architecture, Domain-Calibrated Safety Evaluation, and a Proposed Minimum Safety Stack
evidence.outcome: Safe-response rate under structured red-team attacks versus commercial baselines
evidence.effect: TLAS-YHCT 100% safe-response rate versus 88.9% and 78.7% for two commercial baselines across 206 attacks
evidence.quote: A structured red-team of 206 attacks—constructed by domain-expert clinician-educators independent of system developers, scored blind by the same experts under a dual IT-security and clinical-education safety criterion—yielded a 100% safe-response rate versus 88.9% and 78.7% for two commercial baselines.

evidence.title: Red Teaming Large Language Models in Medicine: Real-World Insights on Model Behavior
evidence.outcome: Inappropriate LLM responses identified through multidisciplinary red-teaming of clinical scenarios
evidence.effect: 19.8% of 1146 responses labeled inappropriate; GPT-3.5 25.7%, GPT-4.0 16.2%, GPT-4.0 with internet 17.5%. Red teaming with 80 experts surfaced safety, privacy, hallucination, and bias failures.
evidence.quote: Results demonstrate a significant proportion of inappropriate responses across GPT-3.5, GPT-4.0, and GPT-4.0 with Internet (25.7%, 16.2%, and 17.5%, respectively) and illustrate the valuable role that non-technical clinicians can play in evaluating models.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (382 unique prompts x 3 models)

evidence.title: Real-World Evaluation of Large Language Models in Healthcare (RWE-LLM): A New Realm of AI Safety & Validation
evidence.outcome: Correct medical advice and harm rates across iterations after clinician red-teaming feedback
evidence.effect: Correct advice improved from ~80.0% (pre-Polaris) to 96.79%, 98.75%, 99.38% (Polaris 1.0–3.0); minor-harm advice fell 1.32% to 0.13% and 0.07%; severe harm eliminated (0.00%).
evidence.quote: Performance metrics demonstrated substantial safety improvements between iterations, with correct medical advice rates improving from ∼80.0% (pre-Polaris), to 96.79% (Polaris 1.0), to 98.75% (Polaris 2.0) and 99.38% (Polaris 3.0).

evidence.title: Red teaming ChatGPT in medicine to yield real-world insights on model behavior
evidence.outcome: Proportion of inappropriate LLM responses found via adversarial red teaming with clinicians and students
evidence.effect: Of 376 unique prompts (1504 responses), 20.1% were inappropriate (GPT-3.5: 25.8%; GPT-4.0: 16%; GPT-4.0 with Internet: 17.8%); GPT-4o 20.4% inappropriate.
evidence.quote: Of 376 unique prompts (1504 responses), 20.1% were inappropriate (GPT-3.5: 25.8%; GPT-4.0: 16%; GPT-4.0 with Internet: 17.8%).

evidence.title: MHSafeEval: Role-Aware Interaction-Level Evaluation of Mental Health Safety in Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Harm discovery by adversarial multi-turn evaluation versus static benchmarks for mental health LLMs
evidence.effect: Adversarial multi-turn agent-based evaluation revealed substantial role-dependent and cumulative safety failures missed by static benchmarks, and improved failure-mode coverage and diagnostic granularity. No numbers are available in the text provided.
evidence.quote: Our results reveal substantial role-dependent and cumulative safety failures that are systematically missed by existing static benchmarks, and show that our framework significantly improves failure-mode coverage and diagnostic granularity.

evidence.title: Beyond Benchmarks: Dynamic, Automatic And Systematic Red-Teaming Agents For Trustworthy Medical Language Models
evidence.outcome: Ability of automated adversarial red-teaming agents to uncover LLM vulnerabilities, validated against clinicians
evidence.effect: Adversarial agents, validated against board-certified clinicians with high concordance, surfaced high failure rates: privacy leaks in 86% of scenarios, bias priming altering recommendations in 81%, hallucination rates above 74%.
evidence.quote: Validated against board-certified clinicians with high concordance, a suite of adversarial agents autonomously mutates clinical test cases to uncover vulnerabilities in real time.

evidence.title: Red-Teaming Medical AI: Systematic Adversarial Evaluation of LLM Safety Guardrails in Clinical Contexts
evidence.outcome: Harm-eliciting success rate of adversarial red-team prompts against a medical LLM assistant
evidence.effect: 11 of 160 adversarial prompts (6.9%) elicited clinically significant harm; full refusal in 86.2%; authority impersonation succeeded 45.0%, Educational Authority sub-strategy 83.3%; six of eight categories had no successful attacks.
evidence.quote: Of 160 adversarial prompts evaluated against Claude Sonnet 4.5, 11 (6.9%) elicited responses meeting our threshold for clinically significant harm (harm level ≥ 3 on a 0–5 scale).

evidence.title: Large Language Models Are Highly Vulnerable to Adversarial Hallucination Attacks in Clinical Decision Support: A Multi-Model Assurance Analysis
evidence.outcome: LLM elaboration on fabricated details embedded in clinical prompts (adversarial hallucination)
evidence.effect: Hallucination rates ranged from 50% to 82% across models and prompting methods.
evidence.quote: Hallucination rates ranged from 50% to 82% across models and prompting methods.
evidence.sample_unit: model outputs (300 vignettes x 2 lengths x 6 LLMs x 3 conditions... reported as 5,400 outputs)

evidence.title: Current safeguards, risk mitigation, and transparency measures of large language models against the generation of health disinformation: repeated cross sectional analysis
evidence.outcome: LLM safeguards against generating health disinformation under adversarial prompting and jailbreaking
evidence.effect: GPT-4 (ChatGPT), PaLM 2/Gemini Pro (Bard), and Llama 2 generated disinformation blogs without needing jailbreaks; refusal rate only 5% (7 of 150); Claude 2 declined all 130 prompts.
evidence.quote: In contrast, GPT-4 (via ChatGPT), PaLM 2/Gemini Pro (via Bard), and Llama 2 (via HuggingChat) consistently generated health disinformation blogs.

evidence.title: Vulnerability of Large Language Models to Prompt Injection When Providing Medical Advice
evidence.outcome: Undiscovered vulnerabilities to prompt injection and manipulation in commercial LLMs giving medical advice
evidence.effect: Injection succeeded in 94.4% of evaluations at turn 4; even flagship models showed high susceptibility (80-100%).
evidence.quote: In this quality improvement study using a controlled simulation, commercial LLMs demonstrated substantial vulnerability to prompt-injection attacks that could generate clinically dangerous recommendations; even flagship models with advanced safety mechanisms showed high susceptibility.

evidence.title: JMedEthicBench: A Multi-Turn Conversational Benchmark for Evaluating Medical Safety in Japanese Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Model safety under adversarial jailbreak conversations, commercial versus medical-specialized models
evidence.effect: Commercial models maintained robust safety; medical-specialized models showed increased vulnerability, which persisted across Japanese and English versions.
evidence.quote: we find that commercial models maintain robust safety while medical-specialized models exhibit increased vulnerability.

evidence.title: Ethical Risks in Deploying Large Language Models: An Evaluation of Medical Ethics Jailbreaking
evidence.outcome: Jailbreak attack success rate of LLMs on Chinese medical ethics themes
evidence.effect: Jailbreak ASR reached 82.1%, an ASR Gain of over 80 percentage points; five models including Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-4.1 had ASRs of 96% to 100%; Claude-Sonnet-4-Reasoning was most robust.
evidence.quote: A systemic collapse of defenses was observed, whereas models demonstrated high baseline compliance, the jailbreak ASR reached 82.1%, representing an ASR Gain of over 80 percentage points.

evidence.title: Safety boundary maintenance in consumer AI systems responding to pediatric health queries: a cross-platform benchmark evaluation under naturalistic and adversarially pressured conditions
evidence.outcome: Safety Composite Score under adversarial caregiver pressure patterns versus authentic queries
evidence.effect: Adversarial pressure was associated with higher, not lower, scores for all four models; false expertise claims were the most vulnerability-inducing pattern.
evidence.quote: False expertise claims were the most vulnerability-inducing pressure pattern, whereas emotional escalation was associated with the highest scores.
evidence.sample_unit: pediatric health queries (300 authentic caregiver queries and 300 matched adversarial variants)

evidence.title: Cloud-Based and Locally Deployed Language Models in Nursing and Health Care: An AI Act-Aligned Framework
evidence.outcome: Resistance to explicit harmful prompts and progressive jailbreak attempts across LLMs
evidence.effect: DeepSeek-R1, Perplexity Sonar, Mistral Large 2, and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct failed to resist even explicit harmful prompts; Claude 3 Opus resisted both explicit harmful prompts and all jailbreak attempts.
evidence.quote: DeepSeek-R1, Perplexity Sonar, Mistral Large 2, and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct failed to resist even explicit harmful prompts; Claude 3 Opus resisted both explicit harmful prompts and all jailbreak attempts, while demonstrating null sycophancy.

commentary.bottom_line: Eight simulated or benchmark studies suggest that structured red-teaming, especially multi-turn and expert-led testing, finds vulnerabilities that single-turn testing misses, and one pre-post series reported severe-harm advice falling to 0.00% after clinician feedback. No study tested the role of affected-population representatives or whether red-team results fed into governance decisions change patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Eight studies test red-teaming, and all ran in simulated or benchmark settings at evidence levels 4 and 5. Only one measured change after red-team feedback, and it was a pre-post series without a comparator. None included affected-population representatives or linked findings to governance decisions or patient outcomes. The results point the same way, but indirectness and design limits keep certainty very low.

In one study, all 4 high-severity errors appeared in multi-turn tests that single-turn testing missed. After clinician red-team feedback, severe-harm advice fell to 0.00% across 307,000 calls. A hazard study found that injection succeeded in 94.4% of evaluations by turn 4, which suggests red-teams may need multi-turn scenarios.

Two multidisciplinary red-teaming efforts labeled 19.8% of 1,146 responses and 20.1% of 1,504 responses as inappropriate, and one drew on 80 experts. Automated adversarial agents showed high concordance with board-certified clinicians and reported privacy leaks in 86% of scenarios, which suggests automation may lower expert burden. No study reported staff hours or workflow fit.

No study testing red-teaming included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and none used affected-population representatives as testers. Hazard studies in Japanese and Chinese found jailbreak vulnerabilities that persisted across languages, with attack success reaching 82.1%. Red-teaming conducted only in English may miss these failures.

Nine sources endorse the practice. They include NIST AI 600-1, which warns against extrapolating performance from nonsystematic assessments, and a regulatory discussion paper that calls for scoring rubrics validated through qualified expert input. Most endorsements are commentaries. The supplied studies used different probe sets and scoring methods, so their results are not yet comparable across vendors.

One vendor applied red-teaming feedback across three product iterations and 307,000 calls, and correct advice rose from about 80.0% to 99.38%. A 160-prompt set found that 6.9% of prompts elicited clinically significant harm, which suggests targeted probe sets of modest size may be feasible. No study reported cost or staffing.

Authority impersonation succeeded in 45.0% of attempts against a medical assistant. In pediatric caregiver queries, false expertise claims were the pattern most likely to induce vulnerability. These findings suggest red-teams may benefit from patient and caregiver input. No study tested whether red-teaming helps patients reach a human when a tool fails.

commentary.research_gap: No study tested whether adding affected-population representatives to red-teams changes which failures are found. No study tracked whether red-team findings routed through governance altered deployment decisions or reduced harm in live clinical use. No study compared the yield and cost of expert-led, automated, and mixed red-teaming under a shared protocol.
commentary.underserved_note: No study that tested red-teaming included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and none used affected-population representatives as testers. Two hazard studies in Japanese and Chinese found vulnerabilities in non-English use, so the value of red-teaming for these groups remains untested.
